newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore electronics to lag US chip data recovery. [CORRECTED 10:57 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Singapore electronics to lag US chip data recovery. [CORRECTED 10:57 GMT]

text.p: Singapore's sagging electronics sector is not likely to recover until the first quarter of 1997 at the earliest, despite U.S. figures showing a pick-up in the industry in September, industry analysts said on Wednesday.

The U.S. Semiconductor Industry Association said on Tuesday the North American book-to-bill ratio rose to 0.99 in September from a revised 0.93 in August. The ratio means manufacturers received US$99 in new orders last month for very US$100 in shipments.

"The ratio clearly bottomed out in March this year and since then it has been a nice gradual uptrend. Coupled with a nine percent increase in new orders, I think it's the strongest signal to date of the electronics industry turning around," said Liew Yin Sze, chief economist at JM Sassoon.
"This book-to-bill is the first clear industry wide number that suggests we are coming to a close of this inventory correction," he said.
New orders rose to $3.19 billion, up nine percent from a year ago, and shipments inched towards $3.22 billion, up 2.1 percent from August's level.
(Deletes references to Singapore dollars and conversions, making clear figures are in U.S. dollars).
But analysts said the recovery in the Singapore electronics sector would lag the United States by about six months.
"I would expect a lag in Singapore. By the time the new orders get translated into increased output here, it will be six months...sometime in the first quarter of next year," said Liew.

"I think the real rally in the electronics sector will come towards the first quarter of 1997. Then demand will be driven by new technology, new markets and new distribution channels," said Winston Lim, electronics analyst at DBS Securities.
David Toh, electronics analyst at ING Baring, said the Singapore electronics sector would likely see month-on-month improvement in output but little year-on-year improvement.
He said Singapore could stage a "tentative year-on-year" recovery from the second quarter of 1997.
Analysts said they expected mediocre economic figures, by Singapore's normal high standards, for the rest of this year.
"For third quarter and fourth quarter Singapore GDP, I still maintain a forecast of around 5 percent," said Liew.
He saw negative to zero growth in Singapore non-oil domestic exports for the next few months.

Analysts said the expected electronic recovery could help to cushion stock prices' downside risks but added that the Singapore share market could still be undermined by poor sentiment in the property sector.

The Singapore government has introduced a rash of anti-speculative property measures in May. Since then the sector has seen a cooldown in property prices and transactions. Analysts also said the shipyard sector was not doing well.

"People can only hope for an electronic recovery next year. In the meantime we are going to see a lot of bad news with respect to negative growth, negative output, GDP growth of maybe two to three percent...that's going to have a bigger sentiment impact than people looking ahead six months down the road," said an analyst at a foreign broking house.
